newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-MUSTER, TOP SPANIARD STRUGGLE INTO LAST 16.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-MUSTER, TOP SPANIARD STRUGGLE INTO LAST 16.

text.p: Fifth seed Thomas Muster survived a string of minor scares at the Australian Open on Saturday to join a growing band of Spaniards in the last 16.

Muster, a clay court specialist hungry to prove his credentials on the hardcourt of Melbourne Park, had to save a dozen break points against German qualifier Jens Knippschild before winning 6-4 7-6 (7-2) 6-3.
The scoreline disguised a close, grinding baseline battle. The 1995 French Open champion repeatedly clawed his way back from two or three break points down to hold serve.
The Austrian then raced to a 5-0 lead in the third set, before struggling to finish off his opponent.
"It took me a little while to work out his weaknesses, but I am pleased with the way I am playing," Muster told reporters after the match.
"At 5-0 down in the third set, he had nothing to lose and he went for his shots and they mostly went in. There's not much I could do about it other than playing steadily, which is what I did."
The "King of Clay", who is drawn to meet eighth seeded South African Wayne Ferreira or unseeded Italian Renzo Furlan in the next round, joined a growing list of Spaniards into the fourth around.

Spain's top men's player, tenth seeded Albert Costa, overcame a partisan crowd to beat Australian Scott Draper in straight sets on Centre Court in another tough match not borne out by the 6-4 6-2 7-5 scoreline.
Costa was broken in the first and third sets by the unseeded Australian but closed out the crucial points to record his best ever grand slam performance away from the clay courts of Europe.

He joins compatriots Carlos Moya, the event's heart-throb and giant-killer after beating defending champion Boris Becker in the first round, and 14th seed Felix Mantilla in the last 16 -- Spain's best grand slam performance on hardcourt.
Of the four annual grand slam events, the Australian Open's Rebound Ace surface is the closest in terms of speed and bounce to the red clay courts of Spain.
